title: Piggyback Tasks to Make the Most of Your Time
author: Rebecca Lowman
summary: Leaders can maximize efficiency by strategically piggybacking new tasks onto existing, well-established systems and routines. Rather than creating parallel processes or adding meetings, effective leaders identify embedded communication channels, routine duties, and movement patterns already reaching their teams, then layer additional purposes onto these moments without overloading staff or eroding their primary function. This approach—also called habit stacking or pairing—allows for information gathering, messaging reinforcement, relational connection, and quality assurance simultaneously, transforming routine duties into dual-purpose opportunities that preserve both organizational agility and human wellbeing.
points: Look for pre-existing systems already reaching the right people—parents' evening forms, staff meetings, break duties, walking patterns—and gently adapt them to serve a new initiative without creating new administrative burden.

Piggybacking time means sending two leaders to a conference together, not for duplicate learning but for protected planning conversations and relational collaboration that the school day never permits.

Piggybacking duties means keeping light, high-emotional-impact touches during break supervision—a quick check-in on a tired ECT or confirmation of a meeting time—without distracting from vigilance or eroding the primary purpose.
Batch and stack functional tasks (photocopying, reprographics, resource gathering) with relational or reflective work, turning administrative chores into meaningful touchpoints with staff.
quotes: Once you see it, one question has been circling my mind this week: As leaders, are we making the most of the activities we're already doing? Or put another way: where could we piggyback one task onto another?” “We simply piggybacked onto something already working. It was such a small tweak, but it immediately solved three problems: we didn't need a new system, we didn't need more meetings or admin, and we didn't need to ask staff or parents to learn anything new.

When something is routine, embedded, understood and already reaching the right people, it becomes fertile ground for gentle adaptation. These small additions or amendments can support information-gathering, communication, reinforcement of a message, expectation or rule, quality assurance, relational connection, and efficiency.

The Head was explicit: 'The value isn't only in attending the conference with a colleague. It's in your time together; the train journey, the conversations, the planning you never get space for during the school day.' That's piggybacking!

Piggybacking in this instance is neither overloading nor eroding. It is very light touch but packs a punch. The tasks you piggyback onto break duty might include checking in on a colleague, delivering a short simple message verbally, confirming the time of a meeting, or checking in on a student you mentor.” Archived from Rebecca Lowman Substack on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
